newsitem.title: USA: Clinton re-certifies Mexico on drugs.
newsitem.headline: Clinton re-certifies Mexico on drugs.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton, swayed by the need to maintain ties with a border state that is the third largest U.S. trading partner, on Friday certified Mexico as an ally in the drug war despite serious corruption problems.
The decision fuelled a domestic political dispute, including a critic's pledge to try to get Congress to overturn the action.
At the same time, Clinton de-certified Colombia for the second straight year. But officials said Bogota could take action to get the pariah designation reversed within months.

Clinton "decided to grant Mexico a full certification but with firm expectations of further (anti-drugs) progress in the near term," Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said in announcing certification decisions for 32 countries.

She said 23 countries including Mexico were certified as U.S. drug-fighting allies and three -- Belize, Lebanon and Pakistan -- were denied certification but given "national security waivers" sparing them U.S. economic punishments that may accompany decertification.

In addition to Colombia, other countries denied certification in 1997 were Afghanistan, Burma, Iran, Nigeria and Syria, the same as 1996, she said. Failure to be certified can lead to harsh U.S. economic and trade sanctions, as well as a diplomatic black eye.
While admitting the struggle against drugs remained formidable, Washington claimed that overall it made "solid gains" in 1996 against the international narcotics trade.

"Working with our allies in the Western Hemisphere, the US-led effort pressed the drug syndicates at their most vulnerable points. We interrupted their preferred trafficking approaches to the United States, forcing them to shift to longer routes in the eastern Caribbean," the report said.
"We helped the drug source countries to eradicate coca plantations and opium poppy fields," it added.

But, Mexican drug groups now control much U.S.-bound cocaine traffic, crack addiction is common in the hemisphere and amphetamines "are well on their way to becoming the drug control nightmare of the next century," the report said.

Corruption charges against the official leading Mexico's anti-drugs efforts, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, sparked calls in Congress to decertify Mexico. He was accused of taking bribes from a drug kingpin.
Democratic Sen. Dianne Feinstein of California, which borders Mexico, said she would lead an effort to have Congress disapprove Clinton's certification decision.

"Have we received some cooperation from Mexico? Undoubtedly. President (Ernesto) Zedillo and many others are working with us in good faith. But have we received full cooperation? Not even close," she said.

A U.S. official called the Mexico decision a "tough call" that could have gone either way. But Clinton was swayed to certify the neighbouring state because "there really is a lot of progress to point to," the official said.

Officials were also concerned about negating the positive bilateral feelings that accompanied Mexico's early repayment of $40 billion in controversial U.S. loan guarantees and about undermining Clinton's planned visit to Mexico on April 11-12.
Furthermore, U.S. officials said they were concerned that decertifying Mexico would cause such ill-will it would make future anti-narcotics cooperation even more difficult.
Albright, handling her first drug report as secretary of state, recommended the certification, officials said.

Mexican officials have been annoyed at the need to be "graded" by Washington and Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria had suggested decertification could fracture bilateral ties between the two countries, which share a 2,000 mile border.
Albright said six Mexican attorney generals and five drug czars "have come and gone in the last five years without making major headway against drug barons and officials who operate above the law."
The decision on Colombia also stirred intense interest.

"This year, like last year, the president's decision to deny certification to Colomba was the result of our concern that corruption remains rampant at the highest levels of the Colombian government and that senior officials are failing to ... cooperate with us in the fight against drugs," she said.
Washington has accused Colombian President Ernesto Samper of taking millions of dollars in bribes from drug-traffickers to finance his 1994 election campaign.

Colombian Vice President Carlos Lemos Simmonds, who warned the decision threatened to drive U.S.-Colombian ties to a new low, called it "arbitrary and unjust" and said the annual U.S. drug test known as "certification" had lost all credibility.
